hints: At the interior maximum, differentiate $y=\cos x\sqrt{\sin2x}$ and set the derivative to zero.
After clearing the square root, simplify the stationary equation with double- or triple-angle identities to an equation in one trigonometric function.
Use $0\le a\le\pi/2$ and the fact that $M$ is the interior maximum to select the exact value only.
walkthrough:
Differentiate $y = \cos x\sqrt{\sin(2x)}$ with respect to $x$ using the product rule $(uv)' = u'v + uv'$:
$$u = \cos x \implies \dfrac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x} = -\sin x$$
$$v = [\sin(2x)]^{1/2} \implies \dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{1}{2}[\sin(2x)]^{-1/2}(2\cos(2x)) = \dfrac{\cos(2x)}{\sqrt{\sin(2x)}}$$

Form the overall derivative:
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = -\sin x\sqrt{\sin(2x)} + \dfrac{\cos x\cos(2x)}{\sqrt{\sin(2x)}}$$

Place over a single common denominator $\sqrt{\sin(2x)}$:
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{-\sin x\sin(2x) + \cos x\cos(2x)}{\sqrt{\sin(2x)}}$$

Apply the cosine compound angle identity $\cos(A + B) = \cos A\cos B - \sin A\sin B$ with $A = 2x$ and $B = x$:
$$\cos(2x)\cos x - \sin(2x)\sin x = \cos(2x + x) = \cos(3x)$$
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{\cos(3x)}{\sqrt{\sin(2x)}}$$

At the maximum point $M$ where $x = a$, set $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = 0$:
$$\cos(3a) = 0$$

Solve for $a$ in the interval $0 \leqslant a \leqslant \dfrac{\pi}{2}$:
$$\text{For } 0 \leqslant a \leqslant \dfrac{\pi}{2}: \quad 0 \leqslant 3a \leqslant \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$$
$$3a = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \implies a = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$$
$$\left(\text{At } 3a = \dfrac{3\pi}{2}, \; a = \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \text{ which lies on the boundary where } y = 0\right)$$
$$a = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$$

hints: Square the curve carefully to obtain $y^2=\cos^2x\sin2x$.
Use $\sin2x=2\sin x\cos x$ so the integrand becomes suitable for the substitution $u=\cos x$.
Evaluate at $0$ and $\pi/2$, retaining the outer factor $\pi$ and simplifying exactly.
walkthrough:
State the formula for the volume of revolution about the $x$-axis from $x = 0$ to $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$:
$$V = \pi \int_0^{\pi/2} y^2\,\mathrm{d}x$$

Square the equation of the curve $y = \cos x\sqrt{\sin(2x)}$:
$$y^2 = \left(\cos x\sqrt{\sin(2x)}\right)^2 = \cos^2 x\sin(2x)$$

Use the double angle formula $\sin(2x) = 2\sin x\cos x$ to express $y^2$ as an integrable derivative form:
$$y^2 = \cos^2 x(2\sin x\cos x) = 2\cos^3 x\sin x$$

Integrate using the recognition method $\int f'(x)[f(x)]^n\,\mathrm{d}x = \dfrac{[f(x)]^{n+1}}{n+1}$:
$$\text{Since } \dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}[\cos^4 x] = 4\cos^3 x(-\sin x) = -4\cos^3 x\sin x:$$
$$\int 2\cos^3 x\sin x\,\mathrm{d}x = -\dfrac{2}{4}\cos^4 x = -\dfrac{1}{2}\cos^4 x$$

Evaluate the definite integral between the limits $0$ and $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$:
$$\int_0^{\pi/2} 2\cos^3 x\sin x\,\mathrm{d}x = \left[ -\dfrac{1}{2}\cos^4 x \right]_0^{\pi/2}$$
$$\text{At } x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}: \quad -\dfrac{1}{2}\cos^4\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = -\dfrac{1}{2}(0)^4 = 0$$
$$\text{At } x = 0: \quad -\dfrac{1}{2}\cos^4(0) = -\dfrac{1}{2}(1)^4 = -\dfrac{1}{2}$$
$$\int_0^{\pi/2} y^2\,\mathrm{d}x = 0 - \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}$$

Multiply by $\pi$ to obtain the exact volume:
$$V = \pi \times \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$$
